title: Functional Diversity Shifts Across the Ediacaran Period Suggest Multiple Drivers for the Rise of Complex Animals
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

The Ediacaran Period (~635–538.5 Ma) records the initial rise and diversification of animals. While many studies have examined the evolving structure of these early animal communities, far fewer have examined evolving function. Here, we quantify change in functional diversity (i.e., the distribution of ecological traits within assemblages) in marine benthic communities throughout the Ediacaran. These metrics allow us to identify how biotic assemblages responded to ecological, environmental, and spatial pressures to form communities.

Location

Global.

Time Period

575–538.5 Ma.

Major Taxa Studied

Marine macrofauna of the Ediacaran Period.

Methods

Genus occurrence and functional trait data were collected from museum collections and the primary literature. From those data, we assessed paleocommunity and global functional diversity using three indices: functional richness, evenness, and divergence, and used these to reconstruct aspects of trait variation. We then used a Jackknife approach to test how individual traits contributed to each functional diversity index. Finally, we quantified how functional beta diversity changed across the Ediacaran, testing whether spatial variation in functional diversity changed between assemblages.

Results

We found that functional richness and divergence significantly varied between chronostratigraphic ‘assemblages’, following rises and falls in paleocommunity taxonomic richness. We find that no single trait controlled functional diversity patterns across assemblages. However, in the last assemblage of the Ediacaran, we find evidence for increased trait filtering between global and paleocommunity functional richness—a pattern which is most strongly indicated by an increase in functional beta diversity.

Conclusions

We interpret our results as reflecting overlapping patterns of environmental and ecological change, reducing paleo-community functional diversity across different spatial scales. Thus, the balance of pressures operating in tandem across different spatial scales (such as environmental filtering by anoxia and/or ecosystem engineering) may have substantially impacted animal evolution. These pressures and their spatial distribution patterns may have controlled which functional trait combinations survived and which functional groups diversified within the Ediacaran.
